questions.q: Why should you run nvidia-smi and check CUDA availability before launching a serving framework?
options: It is a required legal step for all GPU usage
It catches the most common early failure — insufficient free GPU memory or a missing CUDA environment — before it shows up as a confusing crash later
It permanently increases the GPU's memory capacity
It automatically downloads the model weights
questions.explain: Confirming GPU visibility and free memory up front catches the most common early deployment failure (not enough VRAM) before it surfaces as a harder-to-diagnose crash during model loading.

questions.q: In vLLM's startup logs, what does the "maximum concurrency" line tell you?
options: The maximum number of GPUs the server can use
vLLM's own estimate of how many max-length requests it can run truly concurrently given the KV cache memory it allocated
The total number of requests served since the server started
The model's total parameter count
questions.explain: The maximum concurrency line is vLLM reporting, based on your --max-model-len and allocated KV cache memory, roughly how many full-length requests it could serve simultaneously — worth checking against expected traffic.

questions.q: Why is sending a single successful request not sufficient to call a deployment "done"?
options: A single request can never actually succeed
It confirms correctness (the pipeline works end to end) but says nothing about performance under realistic concurrent load
Single requests always use the wrong model
It bypasses the serving framework entirely
questions.explain: A successful single request verifies the pipeline's correctness, but only a load test under realistic concurrency reveals whether the deployment meets its actual latency and throughput requirements.

questions.q: What should the results of a load test be checked against, according to this lesson?
options: The number of lines in the server's source code
Whatever latency SLO the use case actually needs, at a request rate resembling real expected traffic
The GPU's purchase price
The size of the Docker image
questions.explain: Load-test results (TTFT and TPOT percentiles) should be compared against the latency SLO the actual use case requires, tested at a realistic request rate rather than an arbitrary demo rate.

questions.q: If you deployed the same model via Triton's vLLM backend instead of standalone vLLM, which steps change?
options: All five steps change completely, with nothing in common
Only the install/launch and config steps change (writing config.pbtxt and launching tritonserver); environment checks, verification, and load-testing stay conceptually the same
Only the GPU hardware changes
Nothing changes at all, including the launch command
questions.explain: Deploying via Triton swaps the install/launch step for writing a config.pbtxt and launching tritonserver against a model repository, but the environment checks, correctness verification, and load-testing steps remain conceptually the same.
